title: Valve Internship 2027–2028: Why Valve Doesn’t Hire Interns & What to Do Instead
summary: Valve doesn't offer traditional internships, here’s why, what Valve looks for instead, and how to build a path toward working at the company behind Steam and Half-Life.
body_text: Valve Internship 2027–2028: Why Valve Doesn’t Hire Interns & What to Do Instead Last updated: July 2026 Here is the short answer: Valve doesn't hire interns . Their careers page says it plainly: “We don’t hire junior-level professionals or offer internships.” Valve runs with roughly 350 employees, zero managers, and zero entry-level roles , generating about $46 million in revenue per employee , the most revenue-efficient gaming company in the world. That flat, senior-only structure is exactly why no internship program exists. But “Valve internship” is one of the most-searched terms in gaming careers, so this guide does the next best thing: it explains what Valve actually looks for, how their hiring works, and what to do right now to build the resume that gets you there someday. Quick Facts Fact Detail Internship program? No. Valve explicitly states: "We don’t hire junior-level professionals or offer internships" Application window N/A, no internship cycle. Full-time roles are posted year-round at valvesoftware.com/en/jobs Rolling? N/A for internships. Full-time openings are accepted on a rolling basis with no deadline Eligibility (full-time) Years of professional experience (community consensus: 5+), deep expertise, broad skill sets, self-direction Structure Flat, no managers, no job titles, employees choose their own projects Compensation (full-time) Software Engineer median: $375K total comp (Levels.fyi); company-wide median: $217K Location Bellevue, WA only, all roles are in-person at Valve’s sole office Employee count ~350 employees across 11 departments Glassdoor rating 4.4/5 from 75 reviews; 85% would recommend; Compensation & Benefits rated 4.9/5 Valve has no internship program, no application window, and no entry-level pipeline. Every role requires years of professional experience. The path to Valve runs through other companies first. Valve wants years of professional experience before they will talk to you. Externships are short, remote professional experience programs where you finish a real project with a real company, the kind of portfolio evidence that starts building the track record Valve eventually wants to see. The NVIDIA AI & Machine Learning Externship and the Unity Game Design Externship build exactly the technical depth gaming companies look for. Explore all Externships . What Is a Valve Internship? There is no Valve internship, and there never has been one as a formal program. Valve Corporation, the company behind Steam, Half-Life, Counter-Strike, Dota 2, Portal, the Steam Deck, and the upcoming Deadlock, operates with a flat organizational structure where every employee chooses their own projects, desks are on wheels, and compensation is set by peer review. That structure requires people who are already experts. Valve’s own words: they seek “highly skilled folks who’ve been in their industry for a few years and can introduce new types of knowledge and expertise.” With a 4.4 out of 5 on Glassdoor , 85% of employees recommending it, and revenue per employee exceeding $46 million, it's one of the most desirable and most selective employers in gaming. But the path in doesn't start with an internship, it starts with years of proven work elsewhere. When Do Valve Internship Applications Open for 2027–2028? Since Valve has no internship program, this timeline isn't about application deadlines. Instead, it maps what you should be doing right now to build the multi-year track record Valve requires before they will consider you for a full-time role. The community consensus is clear: Valve hires senior professionals with 5+ years of industry experience. Your timeline is measured in years, not semesters. Now · Summer 2026 you're HERE Accept the reality: Valve will not hire you as a student. Use this clarity to build strategically. Land internships at companies that do hire interns, Riot Games, Epic Games, Blizzard, EA, Ubisoft, or Bungie, and start building the shipped-product portfolio Valve wants to see. A remote Externship in game design, AI/ML, or software engineering gives you a real company project to put on your resume before fall recruiting at other studios opens. Junior & senior year (2027–2028) Stack industry internships. Valve values breadth plus depth, so seek roles where you ship something: a game feature, a tool, a system. Contribute to open-source game engines or build and release your own mods. Document everything. First 2–3 years post-graduation Take a full-time role at a studio or tech company where you can own projects end-to-end. Valve looks for people who have introduced “new types of knowledge and expertise” to their teams, become that person at your first employer. Year 5+ · When you’re ready EXPECTED With 5+ years of professional experience and a portfolio of shipped work, you meet the profile Valve describes. Apply at valvesoftware.com/en/jobs , where openings are posted year-round across 11 departments. The average interview process takes about 13 days. Why You Must Apply the Week Applications Open There is no application window to time. But there is a different kind of urgency: the gaming internship slots at companies that do hire interns fill on their own calendars. Riot Games runs 100–150 summer intern positions; Epic Games, Blizzard, EA, and Ubisoft all recruit on fall timelines. If Valve is the long-term goal, these are the stepping stones, and they have their own deadlines. Build the experience Valve wants to see, one internship and one shipped project at a time. Which Valve Internship Programs Should You Target? Valve doesn't offer internship programs. But understanding how Valve organizes its work helps you plan which skills to build. Valve’s 11 departments represent the disciplines they hire for, all at the senior level. Department Focus Hiring level What they look for Software Engineering Steam platform, game engines, tools Senior only Systems programming, multiplayer/networking, Source 2 engine experience Game Design Gameplay, level design, narrative Senior only Shipped titles, deep understanding of player psychology Art 3D character, environment, concept art Senior only AAA-quality portfolio with shipped game credits Hardware Steam Deck, Valve Index, controllers Senior only Consumer electronics, embedded systems, industrial design Product Design UX/UI for Steam and games Senior only Product thinking, interaction design for millions of users Technical Infrastructure Backend systems, data, DevOps Senior only Large-scale distributed systems, Steam’s 67M+ monthly users All 11 departments (also including Audio, Business Development, Finance, Legal, and Customer Support) are listed at valvesoftware.com/en/jobs . Notice the pattern: every role assumes years of industry experience and shipped work. What Are the Eligibility Requirements? Since Valve doesn't offer internships, these are the requirements for full-time employment, the only hiring path that exists: • Experience level: years of professional experience in your field. Community consensus on Reddit and Glassdoor is 5+ years minimum, though Valve doesn't publish an exact number. • Degree: no specific degree or credential is required. Valve explicitly says they don’t require “specific credentials or qualifications.” Portfolio and shipped work matter more than diplomas. • Location: must work in-person in Bellevue, WA, USA. There is no remote option. Valve’s careers page states: “We work together in person, in Bellevue, WA, USA.” • Self-direction: Valve’s flat structure means no one assigns your work. You must be able to identify high-value projects and drive them independently. Why Does Valve Only Hire Seniors? Valve’s flat structure is the reason. With no managers, no job titles, and no hierarchy, every employee must be self-directed enough to choose their own projects and experienced enough to execute them without guidance. Junior employees need mentorship infrastructure that Valve’s structure doesn't provide. As one Reddit commenter put it: “Valve runs super agile with only about 350 members of staff. They might like keeping everything inside or only hiring really top quality candidates.” The $46 million revenue per employee proves the model works, but only with people who are already experts. What Skills Does Valve Look For, and How Do You Build Them? Valve’s active job listings and community reports reveal a consistent picture of what they value. Technical excellence in your domain is table stakes, what separates successful candidates is the breadth to work across disciplines and the business sense to prioritize what matters. In Valve’s flat structure, you need to be your own product manager, your own project lead, and your own quality bar. What Valve looks for in interns Skills across 11 Valve intern & analyst job descriptions · Valve job listings and Glassdoor interview reports, 2025–2026 Deep domain expertise (5+ years) 11 of 11 Shipped products or major contributions 9 of 11 Self-direction & project ownership 8 of 11 Cross-discipline collaboration 7 of 11 Business acumen & product sense 6 of 11 Technical problem-solving 6 of 11 Communication & teamwork 5 of 11 Adaptability & fast learning 4 of 11 Method: qualitative analysis of Valve's 11 department job descriptions, Glassdoor interview reports (46 interviews), and Reddit community discussions about Valve's hiring criteria. Counts represent relative frequency of mention, not exact JD counts. How Is Demand for Gaming Interns Moving Right Now? Gaming industry intern hiring: July 2026 Across major gaming studios with active internship programs · aggregate market signal ▲ Riot Games runs 100–150 summer intern positions annually, one of the largest programs in gaming ★ Epic Games, EA, Blizzard, Ubisoft, and Bungie all maintain formal internship pipelines with fall recruiting windows = Gaming-adjacent tech (Unity, Unreal, cloud gaming) offers internships that build the same skill sets Valve values Valve doesn't participate in this market, but the companies that do are exactly where Valve recruits its senior talent from. Your gaming internship at Riot or Epic is the first leg of a multi-year path to Valve. Method: public career pages of major gaming studios reviewed July 2026. Riot Games intern count from official university programs page. Build These Skills Before You Apply You can't intern at Valve, but you can build the exact skills their job listings demand through remote Externships that put real projects on your portfolio. Skill (from real JDs) JD evidence Externship that builds it Game engine & systems programming Software Engineering dept: Source 2 engine, multiplayer networking, tools development Software Engineering Externships AI / ML & data systems Technical Infrastructure dept: recommendation engines, anti-cheat, matchmaking systems AI & Machine Learning Externships Product design & UX Product Design dept: UX/UI for Steam platform serving 67M+ monthly users Product Design Externships A finished Externship project is exactly the kind of “shipped work” evidence that separates your resume at Riot, Epic, or EA, the studios where you build the 5+ years of experience Valve eventually wants to see. What Is the Valve Application and Interview Process Like? Since there is no internship process, here is how Valve’s full-time hiring works, based on Glassdoor reports and Reddit community accounts: 1. Apply at valvesoftware.com/en/jobs with your resume and a description of how you would apply your expertise at Valve. Openings are posted year-round across 11 departments. Many applicants report never hearing back, Valve only contacts candidates whose skills match current needs. 2. Resume screening. Valve looks for proven senior-level experience and shipped work. There is no recruiter phone screen or automated filter described in community reports, your application either matches or it doesn’t. 3. Pair interviews. All Valve interviews use a two-interviewer format. Candidates go through a full day of back-to-back pair interviews covering technical skills, business acumen, cultural fit, and personality. Interviewers assess not just ability but whether you can thrive in the flat structure. 4. Decision. The average process takes about 13 days from first interview to decision. Valve evaluates technical prowess, thought process, and “how you tackle a problem while optimizing for what is best for business.” There is no online assessment, no coding challenge stage, and no campus recruiting. The process goes directly from application to pair interviews. Glassdoor reports rate the interview difficulty as moderate, but add that “your answers need to be very strong, and that is where the difficulty lies.” What Students on Reddit Say Three Reddit threads capture the reality of trying to work at Valve. We don’t offer junior-level positions or internships, but are looking for highly skilled folks who’ve been in their industry for a few years. r/DotA2 official Valve statement quoted in thread · read the thread Valve don’t do internships or co-ops. Valve exclusively hire senior people with 5+ years or more of experience at senior level in entertainment. r/valve community response, paraphrased · read the thread In order to get into Valve you have to essentially be a skilled industry veteran. Someone who is multi-faceted. r/valve community discussion, paraphrased · read the thread If Valve Doesn’t Hire Interns, What Should You Do Right Now? Three moves, all executable this summer. First, accept the timeline: Valve is a 5-to-10-year goal, not a summer plan. That clarity is freeing because it tells you exactly what to optimize for. Second, intern where interns are welcome. Riot Games, Epic Games, Blizzard, EA, Ubisoft, and Bungie all run formal programs and they build the shipped-game experience Valve wants on your resume. Apply to their fall 2026 windows for summer 2027. Third, build a portfolio that proves you can ship. Contribute to open-source game engines, release mods, finish game jams, or complete a remote Externship in software engineering or game design. Valve’s flat structure means every employee is a self-starter who drives their own work, your portfolio is the first proof that you can do that. What Other Companies Should You Consider? These companies do what Valve doesn't: hire interns. If your long-term goal is Valve, these are the stepping stones. Riot Games 100–150 summer interns; strong engineering and design programs Careers site Epic Games Unreal Engine maker; internships in engineering, art, and design Careers site Blizzard Entertainment large intern class across game design, engineering, and art Careers site Electronic Arts (EA) one of the biggest intern programs in gaming, global offices Careers site Each of these studios hires the kind of junior talent Valve doesn't, and many Valve employees’ resumes include time at exactly these companies. Your internship at Riot or Epic is the first chapter of the story that ends at Valve. FAQ Does Valve offer summer internships for 2027? No. Valve explicitly states on its careers page: “We don’t hire junior-level professionals or offer internships.” This policy has been consistent for years. Valve only hires experienced professionals, typically with 5+ years of industry experience. If you dream of working at Valve, focus on building several years of professional experience at other studios or tech companies first. Has Valve ever had interns? Only as rare, one-off exceptions. In 2011, one high school graduate completed a summer web development internship through a personal connection. In 2013, Valve launched “Pipeline,” a small educational experiment with ten high school students. Neither became a recurring program, and Valve’s official policy remains no internships. What does it take to get hired at Valve? Valve seeks “highly experienced collaborators who are the best at what they do.” You need years of professional experience (community consensus is 5+ years), deep expertise in your discipline, broad complementary skills, and the self-direction to thrive in Valve’s flat, no-managers structure. A strong portfolio demonstrating shipped products is essential. What is Valve’s interview process like? All Valve interviews use a pair format with two interviewers per session. Candidates go through a full day of back-to-back pair interviews covering technical skills, business acumen, and cultural fit. The average process takes about 13 days. Interviewers assess not just technical ability but whether you can work autonomously in Valve’s flat organization. What is Valve’s flat organizational structure? Valve has no managers, no bosses, and no traditional job titles. Every employee chooses their own projects and can switch at any time. Desks are on wheels so teams can physically reconfigure. Compensation is set by peer review. This structure means Valve needs self-directed experts, which is the key reason they avoid hiring junior talent. How much do Valve employees make? Valve pays exceptionally well. Software engineers earn a median total compensation of $375,000 per year (Levels.fyi). Full-time perks include an annual all-expenses-paid Hawaii trip for employee and family, on-site gym with personal training, untracked PTO, and comprehensive benefits. Revenue per employee exceeds $46 million. What are the best alternatives if I want a gaming internship? Companies with formal internship programs include Riot Games (100–150 summer positions), Epic Games, Blizzard Entertainment, Electronic Arts, Ubisoft, and Bungie. These give you the industry experience Valve eventually wants on your resume. Building a strong portfolio with shipped game projects, mods, or game jam entries is another proven path. What skills should I build to eventually work at Valve? Based on Valve’s job listings: game engine development (Source 2), multiplayer and networking systems, 3D character and environment art, VR/AR technology, Steam platform engineering, and hardware design (Steam Deck). Build deep expertise in one area through professional experience at other companies, that is the most realistic path to Valve. Valve is a long-term goal, not a summer application. The path there runs through years of shipped work at studios that do hire interns. Start building that track record now: a remote Externship in game design, software engineering, or AI/ML turns “interested in gaming” into a finished project your next application can point at. About the Author Bifei Wang has spent 17 years focused on human flow and the growth of young professionals, spanning international education, career training and coaching, and recruitment process outsourcing. Over 7 years at Extern, he has had one-on-one sessions with thousands of students exploring careers in consulting, finance, tech, marketing, and data, giving him a firsthand view of how the job market has shifted for early-career professionals and what it actually takes to break in.

title: Sizing the ETF Opportunity: Active ETFs Move to Center Stage
summary: For analysts, nothing is more satisfying than raising long-term forecasts that had once seemed aggressive, if not unattainable. That’s where we find ourselves today with U.S. Exchange-Traded Funds’ assets under management. Citi Research explores U.S. ETFs’ more mature growth phase in this new Must C report.
body_text: Must C: Sizing the ETF Opportunity — Active ETFs Move to Center Stage Download Here A new Citi Research report from a team of strategists led by Drew Pettit explores how the growth of U.S. Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) has exceeded the team’s most optimistic expectations, with the main driver organic inflows and not just strong risk-asset returns. Given this reality, the team now revisits its forecasting framework in its new Must C report, updating its aggregate projections for U.S. ETF assets under management (AUM). A year ago, we laid out our roadmap to the next $10 trillion in U.S. ETF assets. Our core thesis was straightforward: ETFs would continue to take share from mutual funds as professional product innovation expanded access to more precisely engineered investment solutions. Central to that view was a slow burn battle for the core of asset allocation itself, where active approaches would begin to reclaim share from traditional index strategies. We saw this shift as driven by growing awareness of the idiosyncrasies embedded in concentrated and widely followed equity benchmarks, pushing investors toward more differentiated, outcome oriented solutions. In fixed income and other asset classes, the story was already unfolding — index approaches often overlooked or underweighted entire segments that offered distinct return streams. Active ETFs benefited directly from this gap, especially as liquidity ecosystems improved, democratized access, and, in some cases, created entirely new investable universes. In our early Must C research (see Sizing the ETF Opportunity: From Passive Revolution to Active Evolution ), we highlighted ETF encroachment on mutual funds, particularly outside of defined contribution channels. Importantly, we never viewed this as simply another wave of passive adoption. Instead, we saw the ETF wrapper becoming the preferred vehicle for active differentiation across asset classes, strategy design, and newly accessible corners of the global opportunity set. While those views were clearly bullish, the industry’s recent growth has exceeded even our most optimistic expectations, with this growth driven largely by organic inflows rather than just strong risk asset returns. Given this reality, we’re revisiting our forecasting framework and updating our aggregate U.S. ETF AUM projections. These are our current scenarios: Base case: $25 trillion in 2030, $42 trillion in 2035. Growth continues but naturally decelerates as the industry matures, with a more balanced mix of flows and returns. Bull case: $32 trillion in 2030, $73 trillion in 2035. Overall growth rates resemble the past decade, with organic flows remaining the dominant driver alongside strong market performance. Bear case: $20 trillion in 2030, $23 trillion in 2035. New forms of investment funds or investment technologies disrupt the ETF industry, much as ETFs disrupted mutual funds. Growth is largely a function of returns, offsetting outflows in later years — a scenario similar to what we see with mutual funds today. Recent annual U.S. ETF AUM have slightly exceeded our prior bull case. A modeling change reflects this: We now project flows as a percentage of beginning of year AUM rather than extrapolating monthly run rates, which better captures compounding effects in a larger industry. Historically, U.S. ETF AUM has grown at a remarkable 20% annualized pace, with roughly 60% coming from flows. In our base case, we assume meaningful deceleration in flow driven growth as the asset base expands, combined with some minor deceleration in returns. That produces a more even organic inorganic growth split. In the bull case, flows continue to outpace returns as the primary contributor, even while acknowledging ETFs are no longer an early stage industry. In the bear case, the setup increasingly resembles today’s mutual-fund complex, with returns often offsetting negative outflows. Over time, we expect flows as a percentage of AUM to naturally decelerate. Recent years surprised to the upside due to innovation across cryptocurrencies, collateralized loan obligations, and equity derivatives, aided by a more permissive ETF launch environment. When standardized by AUM, however, exponential dollar growth translates into a linear decline in flow intensity — exactly what we’d expect from a maturing industry. Our base case reflects the 10 year historical trend, excluding 2024 and 2025. On returns, aggregate U.S. ETF performance has closely mirrored a globally diversified 60/40 portfolio, averaging 7.3% annualized during the past decade. That serves as the anchor for our assumptions: 6% in our base case, 8% in our bull case, and 4% in our bear case. These sit comfortably within long run historical distributions and imply some modest conservatism amid today’s valuation and rate environment. Ultimately, our earlier forecasts proved conservative because flows, not markets, did the heavy lifting. By reframing growth in terms of flows relative to AUM, we arrive at higher — but we believe more realistic — long term estimates. To us, $25 trillion in U.S. ETF assets by the end of this decade looks clearly attainable, with more than $40 trillion plausible over the next 10 years as innovation continues within an increasingly mature industry. A redacted public version of our new report, Must C: Sizing the ETF Opportunity — Active ETFs Move to Center Stage, is available here .

Non-GAAP Financial Measures Our reported results are presented in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (“GAAP”). We also disclose Funds From Operations (“FFO”), Adjusted Funds From Operations (“AFFO”), and Pro Forma Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (“Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA”), all of which are non-GAAP financial measures. We believe these non-GAAP financial measures are useful to investors because they are widely accepted industry measures used by analysts and investors to compare the operating performance of REITs. FFO, AFFO, and Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA do not represent cash generated from operating activities and are not necessarily indicative of cash available to fund cash requirements; accordingly, they should not be considered alternatives to net income or loss as a performance measure or cash flows from operations as reported on our statement of cash flows as a liquidity measure and should be considered in addition to, and not in lieu of, GAAP financial measures. We compute FFO in accordance with the definition adopted by the Board of Governors of the National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts, or NAREIT. NAREIT defines FFO as GAAP net income or loss adjusted to exclude real estate related depreciation and amortization, as well as extraordinary items (as defined by GAAP) such as net gain or loss from sales of depreciable real estate assets, impairment write-downs associated with depreciable real estate assets and impairments associated with the implementation of current expected credit losses on commercial loans and investments at the time of origination, including the pro rata share of such adjustments of unconsolidated subsidiaries. To derive AFFO, we further modify the NAREIT computation of FFO to include other adjustments to GAAP net income related to non-cash revenues and expenses such as loss on extinguishment of debt, amortization of above- and below-market lease related intangibles, straight-line rental revenue, amortization of deferred financing costs, non-cash compensation, and other non-cash adjustments to income or expense. Such items may cause short-term fluctuations in net income or loss but have no impact on operating cash flows or long-term operating performance. We use AFFO as one measure of our performance when we formulate corporate goals. To derive Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA, GAAP net income or loss is adjusted to exclude extraordinary items (as defined by GAAP), net gain or loss from sales of depreciable real estate assets, impairment write-downs associated with depreciable real estate assets and impairments associated with the implementation of current expected credit losses on commercial loans and investments at the time of origination and/or payoff, and real estate related depreciation and amortization including the pro rata share of such adjustments of unconsolidated subsidiaries, non-cash revenues and expenses such as straight-line rental revenue, amortization of deferred financing costs, loss on extinguishment of debt, above- and below-market lease related intangibles, non-cash compensation, other non-cash income or expense, and other non-recurring items such as disposition management fees and commission fees. Cash interest expense is also excluded from Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA, and GAAP net income or loss is adjusted for the annualized impact of acquisitions, dispositions and other similar activities. FFO is used by management, investors and analysts to facilitate meaningful comparisons of operating performance between periods and among our peers primarily because it excludes the effect of real estate depreciation and amortization and net gains or losses on sales, which are based on historical costs and implicitly assume that the value of real estate diminishes predictably over time, rather than fluctuating based on existing market conditions. We believe that AFFO is an additional useful supplemental measure for investors to consider because it will help them to better assess our operating performance without the distortions created by other non-cash revenues or expenses. We also believe that Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA is an additional useful supplemental measure for investors to consider as it allows for a better assessment of our operating performance without the distortions created by other non-cash revenues, expenses or certain effects of the Company’s capital structure on our operating performance. FFO, AFFO, and Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA may not be comparable to similarly titled measures employed by other companies. GAAP requires that the Sale-Leaseback and Sales-Type Lease Properties and the value of participation obligation interests sold (the “Participation Obligations Sold”) for which sale accounting was not achieved be accounted for as financing arrangements. Accordingly, for GAAP purposes, the Sale-Leaseback and Sales-Type Lease Properties and Participation Obligations Sold are included in the Company’s Commercial Loans and Investments segment. However, for statistical purposes, the Company excludes the Sale-Leaseback and Sales-Type Lease Properties and the Participation Obligations Sold. title: US Air Force awards Leidos ISR operations support task order worth up to $717 million
body_text: RESTON, Va. (July 28, 2026) – As global threats become more complex, contested and fast-moving, U.S. airmen need timely intelligence that is trusted and operationally relevant. Leidos (NYSE: LDOS) has been awarded a new task order by the U.S. Air Force's Air Combat Command (ACC) Acquisition Management and Integration Center (AMIC) to continue delivering intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) operations support for ACC. The task order has a total potential value of approximately $717 million if all options are exercised. It includes a one-year base period with four one-year options. Work will be performed at more than 35 locations in the United States and overseas, positioning Leidos personnel alongside U.S. Air Force mission partners at the point of need and reinforcing the company’s role as an embedded partner in day-to-day mission execution. Leidos has supported this mission as the prime contractor since 2019. The new task order extends that partnership at a time when military leaders need accurate, timely information to assess threats and support operations across air, space, cyber and intelligence missions. “Airmen operate in an environment where decisions often depend on the speed, quality and clarity of intelligence,” said Jason McCarthy, Leidos senior vice president, Airborne & Mission Solutions. “Since 2019, our team has worked alongside Air Combat Command to provide mission-focused ISR support, training and analysis. This next phase of work builds on that foundation with the insight and operational expertise needed to help Airmen assess threats, prepare for missions and support operations around the world.” Under the task order, Leidos will provide subject matter expertise, intelligence analysis, threat mitigation, ISR operations support, training, and mission support services for ACC headquarters, subordinate Numbered Air Forces, centers, and wings. This work reflects Leidos' NorthStar 2030 commitment to helping Department of War customers maintain combat-ready forces and defeat evolving global threats. Headquartered at Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Hampton, Virginia, ACC is one of the U.S. Air Force’s major commands and serves as a primary provider of combat air, space, cyber and intelligence capabilities to America’s warfighting commands. ACC AMIC provides acquisition services that support mission-focused capabilities across the command. About Leidos Leidos is an industry and technology leader serving government and commercial customers with smarter, more efficient digital and mission innovations. Headquartered in Reston, Virginia, with approximately 50,000 global employees, Leidos reported annual revenues of approximately $17.2 billion for the fiscal year ended January 2, 2026. title: Life of an inference request (vLLM V1): How LLMs are served efficiently at scale
summary: vLLM is an open-source inference engine that serves large language models. We deploy vLLM across GPUs and load open weight models like Llama 4 into it. vLLM sits at the intersection of AI and systems programming, so we thought that diving into its details might interest our readers.
body_text: Life of an inference request (vLLM V1): How LLMs are served efficiently at scale June 27, 2025 · 10 min read Junhao Li Senior Software Engineer Ubicloud is an open source alternative to AWS. We offer managed cloud services that build on top of PostgreSQL, Kubernetes, vLLM, and others. ‍ ‍ vLLM is an open-source inference engine that serves large language models. We deploy multiple vLLM instances across GPUs and load open weight models like Llama 4 into them. We then load balance traffic across vLLM instances, run health checks, and do upgrades. Our customers consume our managed service by sending their prompts to our API endpoints. This endpoint also determines the vLLM instance that serves their prompt. vLLM sits at the intersection of AI and systems programming, so we thought that diving into its details might interest some of our readers. In this blog post, we describe how an inference request travels through vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible API server and core engine. We also provide key code pointers. We assume readers are already familiar with the transformer architecture and large language models. If you're not, we highly recommend this video by OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy. We will focus on the new V1 architecture of vLLM and how it achieves state-of-the-art text generation performance. If you're looking for the V0 behavior or multi-modal inference, please refer to other vLLM documentation. Terminology We use the following terms throughout this blog. These terms also align with what is used in vLLM’s codebase and documentation: Request: An incoming chat completion message from the client, formatted in the OpenAI-compatible format . Sequence: The combined stream of prompt and response tokens associated with a request. Except in special cases, a single request typically corresponds to one sequence. Sequence is sometimes used interchangeably with Request in both the codebase and this blog post. Batching: The process of grouping multiple requests together into a single forward pass through the model to maximize GPU utilization. Prefill: The stage in which the model processes the prompt tokens of a new request. It computes the transformer attention and stores the Key (K) Value (V) tensors of the attention for each token and each layer into the KV cache blocks. Decode: The stage in which the model generates the next output token or the output tensor for intermediate layers repeatedly for ongoing requests. It reuses the stored KV cache of all preceding tokens and computes the Query (Q) tensors based on the most recent token. KV Cache: The GPU memory region used to store the transformer attention keys and values for each token in a request. It is managed globally across all requests and devices in vLLM. KV Block: A fixed-size memory unit in the KV cache that holds keys and values for a fixed number of tokens. KV cache is segmented into blocks to minimize memory reads/writes. High Level Architecture Before diving into the request flow, let’s first take a look at the main components of vLLM V1’s serving architecture: AsyncLLM : An asynchronous wrapper around the core engine. The OpenAI-compatible server uses AsyncLLM to submit requests to and retrieve outputs from the EngineCore asynchronously. It communicates with the EngineCore via AsyncMPClient using asynchronous inter-process communication (IPC). It also handles tokenization and detokenization. EngineCore : The core engine that carries out the inference. It is responsible for scheduling, which means batching and allocating tokens for requests. It also executes the model, processing prompt tokens or generating new ones. It’s the heart of vLLM where most of the logic resides. At the core, there is a busy loop that pulls data from an internal input queue and runs an engine step . An engine step includes the scheduling and execution of one forward pass of the model. The results are first pushed to an internal output queue, and then pushed back to the AsyncLLM and the API server. Two additional background threads manage the asynchronous data transfer between the two internal input/output queues and the AsyncLLM over IPC. Scheduler : A component within the engine that handles how multiple requests are batched. The scheduler maintains queues of requests and decides at each step how many tokens to process for each request. ModelExecutor : A component that coordinates the loading and execution of the model across one or more GPU worker processes. Internally, it uses the ray distributed computing library and launches one worker process per GPU device. ModelRunner : Each GPU worker has a ModelRunner that loads the model and executes the forward passes . The ModelRunner takes requests in batches from the scheduler. It processes these requests through the model on all CUDA cores at the same time. It takes care of assembling input tensors and can use optimizations like CUDA graph capture for repeated executions. KVCacheManager : vLLM’s GPU memory management modules, responsible for managing space for the transformer KV tensors on GPU for all requests. It treats GPU memory as a paging system. KV cache is stored in fixed-size blocks, or pages. This allows for efficient dynamic allocation and avoids needing large contiguous memory reservations. The Scheduler uses the KVCacheManager to allocate these blocks and attaches the block IDs to each request. The ModelRunner then uses these IDs when preparing the execution context. This idea of a paged KV cache was proposed by the vLLM authors in the PagedAttention paper and was the genesis of the vLLM project. Receiving the Request – API Server and Async IPC The journey begins when an HTTP request arrives at the vLLM server (e.g. a POST to /v1/chat/completions). The OpenAI-compatible API server handles the HTTP communication and authentication (via the API key, if configured). This server is often launched by running the vllm serve command defined by vllm/entrypoints/cli/serve.py . After validation, the server invokes the AsyncLLM engine to handle the request. In code, this is done by calling the AsyncLLM engine method generate() . The method is given the prompt and a freshly generated request_id to track this request. When the generate() is called, the AsyncLLM performs tokenization with the model’s tokenizer (often from Hugging Face) to convert text to token IDs. Some multimodal input processing also happens at this stage, but for simplicity, we’ll focus on text prompts here. It then sends the request to the EngineCore via AsyncMPClient using asynchronous IPC calls. Then, a background loop at the EngineCore picks up the request from the IPC channel and places it into an internal input queue for scheduling. Note that the AsyncLLM and EngineCore run in different processes. This bypasses Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). It allows CPU-intensive tasks, like tokenization and HTTP communication, to run alongside the GPU-intensive task, the model execution. This maximizes overall throughput. Scheduling and Continuous Batching The Scheduler module is central to vLLM’s ability to achieve high throughput. It keeps track of all requests and orchestrates their progress. The scheduler maintains a waiting deque for requests that are ready to be processed (new or resumed ones) and a running list for requests currently in active generation. In each iteration (cycle) of the engine, it first examines the internal input queue and adds new requests into the scheduler’s waiting deque. It then picks a set of requests to advance, looking at the requests from the running list first, and then the requests from the waiting deque. vLLM uses a continuous batching algorithm. This helps maximize GPU utilization by keeping a full workload within a fixed token budget, a.k.a max_num_batched_tokens . It also ensures fairness in request order and limits the batch to just one forward pass of the model. Here’s a continuous batching example: Suppose we have three requests with 3, 5, and 12 prompt tokens, respectively, and a token budget of 10. In a traditional server, these might be handled sequentially or in fixed-size batches. In vLLM, however, the scheduler could decide in one iteration (Step 0) to feed, for example, 3 prompt tokens from R1, 5 from R2, and 2 from R3 in a single forward pass. Note that it only picks two prompt tokens from R3 due to the token budget of 10. In the next iteration (Step 1), it can continue with the remaining 8 prompt tokens from R3. At the same time, it will start generating 1 token each for R1 and R2. They have finished filling their prompt tokens and are now in the decoding phase. Note that during the prefill phase, all prompt tokens from a request can be processed in one batch. This is possible because the query (Q) tensors, calculated from the tokens immediately before them, are available for each prompt token position. In the decoding phase, however, the immediately preceding token must be decoded iteratively, so we can only process one token at a time per request. The scheduler ensures that all requests complete the prefill phase before entering the decoding phase. During the scheduling phase, the KV cache blocks are also determined. The KV Cache Manager groups tokens into fixed-size chunks and either allocates a new KV block or retrieves an existing KV block for each chunk of the tokens. Note that the actual GPU memory allocation occurs during vLLM initialization. The KV Cache Manager determines the block IDs for the KV caches of each request and attaches these IDs to the request, so they can later be used by the ModelRunners when executing the model. Model Execution – Forward Pass on the GPU Once the scheduler has determined which requests to advance, it invokes the ModelRunners via the ray-based ModelExecutor . This executes the model’s forward pass, either processing the prompt tokens or generating new tokens. All tokens from the selected requests are combined into a single large tensor, a.k.a a batch, and are processed layer by layer through the transformer's weight matrices. At each layer, the three attention tensors, Key (K), Value (V), and Query (Q), of each attention head are computed. Then a final attention output tensor for the layer is computed from these tensors. The K and V tensors are stored for future use, and the output tensor becomes the input for the next layer. This is where GPUs come into play, as they are great at large matrix computations. Each tensor includes data from all batched requests. This allows each matrix operation of these requests to be processed on the GPU in parallel using SIMD(T) (single instruction, multiple data, and multiple threads) across all CUDA cores. For requests in the decoding phase, the output tensor from the final transformer layer produces the logits, which represent the predicted probabilities for the next token. vLLM then applies the sampling or decoding strategy . For each sequence, it looks at the logits and either selects the top token (greedy or deterministic) or samples according to the provided parameters, e.g. temperature. This process produces the next token for each batched request. These tokens are placed into an internal output queue, where a background loop picks them up and sends them back to the AsyncLLM via IPC for output processing. This timeline diagram shows a portion of the forward pass for the DeepSeek R1 Distilled Qwen 32B model that we serve. Within the busy loop of the EngineCore, the model's forward method runs. This method calls the forward methods of each transformer layer. Then, the forward method of each layer calls the FlashAttention module. FlashAttention is a highly optimized function for computing transformer attention. It uses the FlashAttention-3 algorithm. This model contains a total of 64 transformer layers and this timeline diagram shows 3 of them at the bottom. The model runner repeats the forward pass through all 64 transformer layers at each engine step. Output Processing – Streaming Tokens Back The AsyncLLM gets the new tokens from the IPC channel. Then, it processes these tokens by detokenizing them and placing them into an internal output queue. The original caller, the AsyncLLM’s generate() function, will then pick them up and pass them back to the API server. In non-streaming mode, the API handler would accumulate tokens internally until the request is finished and then return the final output. In streaming mode, the handler will send each partial output immediately to the client in chunks like data: {...} Conclusion In this blog post, we’ve gone through the entire life of a vLLM inference request. The journey starts with the API server handing the request to the AsyncLLM, which tokenizes and sends requests to the EngineCore. At EngineCore, the scheduler batches requests. The executor works with the ModelRunner to run forward passes through the attention layers on GPUs. Then, tokens are streamed back to clients. Each component plays a distinct role in this lifecycle, and together they allow vLLM to achieve state-of-the-art serving performance. For AI engineers looking to deploy LLMs, we hope understanding this lifecycle helps in tuning and customizing vLLM. For others, we hope this breakdown provides insight into vLLM's inner workings. By doing so, we aim to demystify how large language models are served efficiently and at scale. References https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm https://blog.vllm.ai/2025/01/27/v1-alpha-release.html

title: NBN Outage Work Hubs for Australian Teams
summary: When the NBN Drops, Work Shouldn’t Stop A video pitch freezes mid-sentence. A payroll file refuses to upload. A client call shifts from confident to chaotic in seconds. For Australian teams that rely on home broadband, a sudden NBN outage can turn a normal workday into a scramble. That is why outage workspaces are becoming […] The post NBN Outage Work Hubs for Australian Teams appeared first on Deskimo .
body_text: When the NBN Drops, Work Shouldn’t Stop A video pitch freezes mid-sentence. A payroll file refuses to upload. A client call shifts from confident to chaotic in seconds. For Australian teams that rely on home broadband, a sudden NBN outage can turn a normal workday into a scramble. That is why outage workspaces are becoming a practical part of remote and hybrid work planning. Whether your team is spread across Sydney suburbs, Melbourne’s inner north, Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide, or regional hubs, backup work locations can protect productivity when home internet fails. Instead of asking employees to tether to unstable mobile data or commute to the head office, companies can prepare a simple “Plan B” that keeps people connected, professional, and focused. Why NBN Outages Hit Hybrid Teams Harder Than They Expect Hybrid work has made Australian organisations more flexible, but it has also shifted more operational risk into employees’ homes. In the office, internet redundancy, meeting rooms, power backup, and IT support are usually managed centrally. At home, a worker may depend on one broadband connection, one router, and one quiet room. When that connection fails, the impact is rarely isolated. One person’s outage can delay a sales demo, interrupt a legal review, stall a finance close, or force a manager to reschedule interviews. For distributed teams, the NBN is no longer just a household utility. It is part of the business infrastructure. The hidden cost of “just work from home” Many teams underestimate the cost of downtime because the interruption looks small on paper. A 90-minute outage may sound manageable, but the knock-on effects can be much larger when the employee is client-facing or working across time zones. Common consequences include: Missed client calls or delayed responses during critical windows Lower meeting quality due to patchy mobile hotspot connections Confidential conversations moved to cafés or public spaces Employees losing time travelling to the office without warning Managers spending time troubleshooting instead of leading Unplanned reimbursements for coworking, mobile data, or transport Australia’s remote work culture has matured quickly, but many policies still assume that home is always available as a reliable workplace. The Australian Bureau of Statistics continues to track working-from-home trends, showing that flexible work is now a mainstream feature of the labour market. Teams can review broader workforce patterns through the ABS working arrangements data to understand how common hybrid arrangements have become. Why mobile hotspots are not a complete backup plan Mobile tethering is useful in a pinch, but it is not enough for every role. A hotspot may handle email and chat, yet struggle with multi-person video calls, large file uploads, virtual desktops, cloud design tools, or CRM-heavy workflows. In apartment buildings, underground locations, storm-affected suburbs, or busy CBD areas, mobile performance can also fluctuate. There are also security and professionalism issues. A finance manager joining a confidential call from a noisy café may be “online,” but not truly work-ready. A recruiter interviewing candidates from a public table may be visible and audible to strangers. That is where outage workspaces provide a more dependable alternative: business-grade internet, proper seating, quiet areas, and meeting facilities when home connectivity fails. How Outage Workspaces Fit Into an Australian Business Continuity Plan Business continuity planning often focuses on cyber incidents, power failures, extreme weather, and office access. Yet for hybrid teams, a home internet outage can be just as disruptive to daily operations. A practical continuity plan should include clear instructions for where employees can work if their home connection is unavailable. Outage workspaces are not about replacing the home office. They are about giving employees a fast, approved fallback option. When the NBN drops, staff should not need to ask five people for permission, search online for a nearby café, or guess whether an expense will be reimbursed. What makes a workspace suitable during an outage? Not every alternate location is appropriate. A good outage workspace should support productive work immediately, with minimal setup time and predictable quality. Look for these essentials: Reliable high-speed internet that can support video calls and cloud tools Comfortable desks and ergonomic seating for focused work Quiet areas or call rooms for confidential conversations Power outlets and backup power where possible Convenient locations near residential suburbs, transit routes, and client districts Simple access without long contracts or manual invoicing Clear usage reporting for HR, finance, and operations teams For teams with employees in multiple cities, consistency matters. A worker in Parramatta, South Yarra, Fortitude Valley, Subiaco, or Canberra’s inner south should be able to follow the same process: check availability, book a spot, and keep working. Build outage response around roles, not seniority A common mistake is to reserve backup work options only for executives. In reality, the people most affected by outages may be customer support agents, recruiters, account managers, finance staff, engineers, consultants, and project coordinators. Consider ranking roles by outage sensitivity: Client-critical roles: sales, account management, consulting, legal, advisory, and customer success Operations-critical roles: finance, payroll, scheduling, compliance, and IT support Collaboration-heavy roles: product teams, designers, marketers, recruiters, and managers Deep-work roles: analysts, developers, writers, and researchers who may need stable access to cloud tools This approach helps companies decide who needs instant access to outage workspaces, who can wait a few hours, and who can continue asynchronously. It also avoids the perception that workspace access is a perk rather than a resilience tool. Choosing the Right Work Hubs Before the Next Outage The best time to choose backup work locations is before an outage occurs. Once the connection is already down, employees are under pressure, meetings are approaching, and good decision-making becomes harder. A pre-approved hub network gives everyone a clear path. Australian teams should think beyond CBD coworking. The ideal solution may include neighbourhood workspaces close to where employees live, client-adjacent hubs near meeting locations, and quiet rooms for secure calls. This is especially important in cities where commuting from outer suburbs to a central office can take an hour or more each way. Map employee locations and common outage scenarios Start with a simple location audit. You do not need exact home addresses to plan effectively. Postcode-level data is often enough to identify clusters of employees who would benefit from nearby backup locations. Ask these practical questions: Which suburbs have the highest concentration of hybrid employees? Which roles require reliable video calls every day? Which employees live far from the main office? Which teams work with international clients outside standard Australian business hours? Which locations are most vulnerable to storm disruption, local infrastructure works, or mobile congestion? Employees can check current network issues through the NBN network status page , but a status page alone does not solve the problem. Teams still need a practical place to go when work cannot wait. Prioritise secure calls and professional environments During an outage, the temptation is to find the nearest place with Wi-Fi. That may be a café, library, shopping centre, or hotel lobby. These options can work for light admin, but they are risky for confidential or high-stakes work. Privacy matters for HR conversations, board updates, contract negotiations, medical-adjacent services, legal discussions, financial reviews, and enterprise sales. If employees are expected to handle sensitive information, they need access to spaces designed for professional calls. For deeper guidance on this topic, see secure call pods for Australian hybrid teams . Security is also about behaviour. Provide employees with a short checklist for outage days: Use company-approved VPN and multi-factor authentication Avoid discussing confidential matters in open public areas Use headphones for calls Lock screens when stepping away Confirm that any booked room is suitable for sensitive discussions Practical Playbook: Setting Up Outage Workspaces for Your Team A useful outage plan should be simple enough for employees to follow under pressure. If it requires multiple approvals, manual forms, or manager-by-manager discretion, it will fail when people need it most. Treat outage workspaces like a standard operating procedure, not an ad hoc benefit. The goal is to create a repeatable path from “my NBN is down” to “I am working productively from a suitable nearby hub.” Step 1: Define when employees should use a backup workspace Start by setting clear triggers. This prevents confusion and gives managers confidence that workspace use is legitimate. Examples of reasonable triggers include: Home internet is unavailable for more than 30 minutes during core working hours Mobile hotspot speed is not sufficient for scheduled meetings The employee has a client presentation, interview, or deadline within the next three hours The outage affects a role that is part of payroll, customer support, incident response, or revenue operations The employee cannot work securely from a public venue Be specific, but avoid making the policy overly rigid. A senior consultant preparing for a client workshop may need a workspace immediately, while another employee can shift to offline work for an hour. Step 2: Set budgets, approvals, and reporting Finance teams often worry that flexible workspace access will create uncontrolled spending. That risk is real if employees are left to book whatever they find and expense it later. A better approach is to set clear budgets and use platforms that provide centralised reporting. This is where companies should also watch for hidden costs. When employees pay for cafés, coworking day passes, hotel lounges, or transport out of pocket, workspace spend becomes fragmented and hard to measure. The issue is similar to the broader challenge of shadow workspace spend in hybrid teams , where untracked expenses can quietly grow across departments. A clean policy should answer: Who is eligible to book an outage workspace? What is the daily or monthly usage limit? Can employees book meeting rooms or only desks? Who approves exceptions? How will usage be reported to HR, operations, and finance? For many Australian businesses, the answer is not a large fixed office footprint. It is controlled access to flexible work hubs that employees use only when needed. Step 3: Communicate the plan before a disruption A policy is only useful if employees know it exists. Share the outage process during onboarding, hybrid work refreshers, manager training, and business continuity reviews. Keep the instructions short and easy to find. A simple internal message could say: “If your home NBN connection is down and you have time-sensitive work, check the network status, notify your manager, and book an approved workspace near you. Use a private room for confidential calls and record the reason as ‘connectivity outage’.” Managers should model the behaviour too. If leaders treat backup workspaces as a normal productivity tool, employees are less likely to feel guilty about using them. Local Factors Australian Teams Should Consider Australia’s geography makes workspace resilience different from many other markets. Major cities are spread out, suburban commuting can be time-consuming, and weather events can affect both connectivity and transport. A backup plan that works in Singapore or central London may not fit Western Sydney, outer Melbourne, regional Queensland, or Perth’s northern corridor. That is why outage workspaces should be planned around real travel patterns, not just office addresses. CBD backup is useful, but neighbourhood access is better A central office can be a backup option, but it is not always the fastest one. If an employee in Penrith, Geelong, Joondalup, or Logan loses internet, sending them to a CBD office may cost half a day in travel and fatigue. A closer workspace can preserve both productivity and wellbeing. Near-home and near-client work hubs are especially valuable when employees have meetings across the city. Instead of returning home between appointments or travelling back to the head office, they can use professional spaces close to where work is happening. This also connects with a broader productivity strategy: near-client workspaces that cut dead time . For business travellers, the same principle applies. A consultant arriving in Melbourne for a workshop or a founder visiting Sydney investors should not depend entirely on hotel Wi-Fi. A reliable workspace near the meeting location can keep the day on track. Plan for weather, power, and infrastructure disruption NBN interruptions are not the only risk. Severe storms, flooding, heatwaves, construction works, and power disruptions can affect home-based work. The Bureau of Meteorology provides regular updates and warnings through Australia’s official weather service , which can help operations teams anticipate disruption in affected regions. Some outage events are local and brief. Others are part of broader infrastructure stress. Teams should identify which work hubs offer not only strong internet, but also dependable power and comfortable conditions. Lessons from other Asia-Pacific markets can be useful here, particularly in cities where backup power is a daily business concern. For example, Deskimo’s guide to power backup workspaces for Jakarta teams offers practical thinking that Australian companies can adapt for storm-prone or disruption-sensitive regions. It is also worth creating a hierarchy of fallback options: First option: approved nearby workspace with reliable internet and call facilities Second option: company office or satellite office, if travel time is reasonable Third option: mobile hotspot for low-sensitivity tasks Last resort: public venue for non-confidential work only Making Outage Workspaces Part of a Better Hybrid Work Culture Backup work hubs are not just an IT fix. They are a sign of a mature hybrid culture. When companies acknowledge that home work has real infrastructure limits, they can support employees without forcing everyone back into a fixed office model. The strongest policies balance flexibility, trust, and accountability. Employees get practical options when something goes wrong. Managers get continuity. Finance gets visibility. Clients get a smoother experience. Measure outcomes, not just usage After introducing outage workspaces, track whether the policy is improving the employee and business experience. Usage data is helpful, but it should not be the only metric. Consider reviewing: Number of outage-related workspace bookings by city or suburb Teams or roles with the highest need for backup locations Client meetings saved from cancellation Employee feedback on commute time and workspace quality Reduction in unplanned reimbursements Manager satisfaction with continuity during disruptions This data can help HR and operations teams refine eligibility, budgets, and location coverage. It can also support broader decisions about office footprint, hybrid work expectations, and employee experience. Keep the policy human Connectivity failures are stressful. Employees may already be dealing with children at home, transport delays, bad weather, or urgent deadlines. A good outage policy should reduce anxiety, not add more admin. Use plain language. Make booking easy. Trust employees to make reasonable decisions. Provide guidance for secure work, but avoid turning every outage into a compliance maze. The most effective message is simple: “If your connection fails, you have somewhere professional to go.” That clarity is valuable for remote workers, entrepreneurs, freelancers, and corporate teams alike. Keep Australian Teams Connected When the Unexpected Happens NBN outages are a reality of modern work, but they do not have to derail the day. With the right plan, Australian teams can move from reactive scrambling to calm continuity. The key is to identify suitable outage workspaces in advance, define when they should be used, protect confidential work, and keep spending visible. For hybrid organisations, this is a practical way to strengthen resilience without abandoning flexibility. For freelancers and business travellers, it offers a professional fallback when home, hotel, or mobile internet is not enough. And for managers, it keeps people productive without forcing unnecessary commutes to a central office. If your team depends on reliable connectivity, now is the time to build a backup workspace plan before the next outage hits. To book a workspace or download the free Deskimo app . title: Abundia Global Impact Group, Inc. Anticipates Increased Revenue Generation Opportunity Through Expansion of Technology Rights Under Alterra License Agreement
body_text: Authorizes Abundia to develop two additional plastics recycling sites in the United States HOUSTON, TX, Dec. 15, 2025 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Abundia Global Impact Group, Inc. (NYSE: AGIG ) ("Abundia" or the "Company"), today announces that it has secured additional rights to Alterra Energy's ("Alterra") Advanced Recycling technology to develop and operate two more plastics recycling sites in the United States. "This has greatly expanded Abundia's opportunity in the U.S.," stated Ed Gillespie, Abundia's Chief Executive Officer. "With each additional site, we have the potential to convert up to 160,000 tons of waste plastic per year to approximately 105,000 tons of high-value renewable fuel and chemical product. At today's prices, this amount of product has the potential to generate over $200 million in revenue annually per site. The additional U.S. sites support Abundia in its quest to become one of the largest producers of renewable fuels and chemicals globally." In 2021, Abundia and Alterra entered into a definitive Technology License and Services Agreement, under which Alterra granted Abundia a license to Alterra's liquefaction technology, to design, build, operate and maintain a plant and related processes at designated sites to transform discarded plastic into renewable hydrocarbons. The original license granted rights to Abundia to operate four sites in Europe and the UK, and one site in the U.S. In the updated agreement, Abundia has secured the rights to two additional sites in the U.S., with potential capacity of up to an additional 320,000 tons per year of waste plastic in the United States. This positive development reinforces the shared commitment between Alterra and Abundia to accelerating discarded plastic solutions in the United States and underscores the country's central role in their joint growth strategy. "This milestone highlights the strength of Alterra's technology and our shared long-term vision with Abundia. By advancing this collaboration, we are accelerating replacement of fossil feedstocks in the US," stated Valerio Coppini, Alterra's Chief Commercial Officer. "Together, we are setting a higher standard for technology performance and delivery within the industry. The deepening of our partnership signals strong market trust, and we are excited to shape the next phase of circular solutions with Abundia." About Abundia Global Impact Group, Inc. Abundia Global Impact Group, Inc. (NYSE: AGIG ), formerly Houston American Energy Corp., is a low-carbon energy company focused on converting waste into value. Headquartered in Houston, Texas, we are developing commercial-scale facilities that transform waste plastics and biomass into drop-in fuels and low-carbon chemical feedstocks. Our flagship project at Cedar Port positions Abundia at the center of the Gulf Coast's energy and chemical infrastructure, with access to feedstock supply chains, upgrading partners, and end markets. For more information, please visit www.abundiaimpact.com . About Alterra Energy Alterra is the developer, operator, and licensor of its thermochemical liquefaction process technology that renews discarded plastic back into its original building blocks, thus minimizing reliance on new, fossil-derived materials for the manufacturing of new plastic products. Our Akron, OH plastics circularity facility is the only full-scale, continuous plant of its kind. Through the global deployment of our technology, we are Solving Plastic Pollution®. Read more: https://alterra360.com/ .
